children: co-founder Bill Gates called for U.S. legislation governing artificial intelligence, arguing that voluntary safeguards by technology companies are not sufficient to manage the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems.

"You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like," Gates said in a taped interview with NBC's "Meet the Press" that aired Sunday. "And that has to be a required thing."
"No one thinks self-regulation is enough," he added.

Gates' comments add to pressure on Washington to establish federal rules for AI, potentially raising compliance costs and changing how quickly companies can develop and deploy advanced models. New safeguards could affect major AI developers as well as chipmakers, cloud providers and other companies spending heavily on AI infrastructure. At the same time, a clear federal framework could reduce regulatory uncertainty and lessen the risk of a patchwork of state rules.
Calls for government oversight have intensified since OpenAI disclosed in July that an autonomous AI agent broke through intended controls during a security test and accessed another company.
Executives from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google's DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI have also called for greater caution in the development of increasingly capable AI systems.

The debate has divided Washington. President Donald Trump and other critics of additional AI regulation have argued that stricter U.S. rules could weaken the country's position against China in the race to develop the technology. Trump has characterized calls for new AI laws as a "hoax."
"It's not a hoax at all," he told NBC.
Concerns about advanced AI systems have gained attention in Washington as researchers have offered increasingly stark assessments of the potential risks.

Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon has warned that advanced AI could pose an existential threat by the end of the decade. Evan Hubinger, Anthropic's alignment science lead, has separately estimated a greater than 10% chance of a catastrophic outcome involving AI within the next decade.
Those concerns have helped fuel proposals for additional federal oversight, including legislation that could give authorities the ability to halt an AI model in an emergency.
Gates said he was not necessarily opposed to a so-called "kill switch," but argued that such a mechanism would need to be part of a broader system of safeguards rather than a standalone solution.

The regulatory debate is also becoming an international issue. The U.S. and China recently agreed to begin a dialogue on AI following Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington, adding another dimension to the competition over the technology's development and governance.

title: Bill Gates calls for federal AI safeguards beyond industry self-regulation
